_note: The distribution networks the player lays by hand, socket by socket. Every building that takes part in a network carries SOCKETS for it (`sockets`: how many of each, and which way they face: `in`, `out`, or `any`; an in-line building's in and out carry a `row`, drawn one above the other so its two pipes never cross), and every LINK (a cable, pipe, drain, duct or feed line) plugs one socket into another: an `out` into an `in`, an `any` into anything, and only between the buildings named in `connects`. A socket takes one link — sockets sharing a `pool` are one sleeve on several lines, such as a fan's duct, which takes either air line — so a junction, a cistern or a generator hands out only as many lines as it has sockets. A FEED network (`users`) is the thin last stretch: its hubs' sockets go to every building that draws the network's resource (`power`: anything with a powerDraw or a recipe; `water`: anything that consumes water), each of which has the one `userSocket`. On a network with `taps`, a link may also run from a socket into the middle of another link of its network — a tee — so one line serves several machines. A link costs `linkCost` per level it spans (at least one) and may span at most `maxSpanLevels`. `socketStyle` is how the view draws the sockets (view/networkLayer.js). The graph is read by systems/infrastructure/networkGraph.js; each system settles its own network over it. A network not listed in config infrastructure.enforced is treated as fully laid (every node joined, every hub reaching everywhere) — which is how system tests isolate one network at a time.

networks.name: High-voltage grid
networks.description: The generators' high-voltage cables, out to the junctions. A generator has six high-voltage outputs; a junction takes one feed in. A battery sits in line, one cable in and one out, so batteries chain in series between a generator and a junction; every battery in the chain backs the junction at its end, and no other. When the generators run short, junctions are served in priority order (1 first).
networks._note: Loss scales with cable run from the generator plus the low-voltage drop from the junction to the room, so a shallow level fed from a deep generator pays for every level of cable between.

networks.name: Low-voltage lines
networks.description: The wires from a junction to the rooms it lights. Every room that draws power has one low-voltage socket, and a junction has twelve: plug each room into a junction no more than four levels away, and keep the junction under what it can carry.
networks._note: A room on no wire is off the grid, however close a junction stands.

networks.name: Water mains
networks.description: The water's loop, fresh half, in large pipe. Pumps drive it: a pump sits in line, one pipe in and one out — the reclamation plant's recovered water in, and out up the mains to the cisterns, with fresh groundwater added for what is lost. A cistern has one fresh-water sleeve and a reclamation plant one; to serve several cisterns from one pump, branch a pipe off the main with a tee. A purifier on the way cleans the reclaimed water that passes through it.
networks._note: Pumping upward costs power proportional to lift height, so water costs more the higher people live.

networks.name: Sewer
networks.description: The water's loop, dirty half, in large drain. What a cistern's rooms use comes back to it dirty; its one sewage sleeve carries it on, downhill only, to a reclamation plant, which takes one drain in. Several cisterns drain into one plant by branching their drains off one another's with tees. Sewage with nowhere to go is dumped where it was made and fouls that level's air.
networks._note: Gravity is the whole design: a drain never carries anything up, so the plant belongs at the bottom.

networks.name: Feed lines
networks.description: The thin double pipe from a cistern to each room it serves: water in, and the used water back beside it. Every room that uses water, a home included, has one feed sleeve; a cistern has ten. Plug each into a cistern no more than four levels away.
networks._note: A home's residents drink through its feed line. People with no home drink at the nearest room that has one.

networks.name: Foul-air ducts
networks.description: The first half of the air's loop. A sucking duct fan draws the foul air off the levels it reaches and sends it down a foul-air duct to a scrubber's foul sleeve — or an oxygen garden's, which feeds on it — and on through it. A fan has one duct sleeve, which takes either line; a scrubber and a garden have one foul and one fresh. Branch a duct off another with a tee to gather several fans into one scrubber. Air only moves when the loop is closed: foul ducts into a scrubber or garden, fresh ducts out of it to a blowing fan.
networks._note: Airflow is settled in systems/airQuality/airflow.js, over this network and fresh-ducts together: the air runs sucker -> foul ducts -> scrubber -> fresh ducts -> blower.

networks.name: Fresh-air ducts
networks.description: The second half of the loop. Out of a scrubber or garden, cleaned or breathed into, the air runs along the fresh-air ducts to the blowing duct fans, which push it out onto the levels they reach; a tee in the duct shares it between several fans. A scrubber cleans only the air its ducts carry through it — never the Shaft's air drifting past it; a garden the air does not pass breathes into its own level only.
networks._note: A duct fan may carry both lines. What it does with its own levels is set by suck or blow; air can still pass through it on either line.
